tool.name: Maven
tool.tagline: Convention-driven build and dependency manager for Java projects, defined by the POM
tool.description: Apache Maven builds Java projects from a declarative pom.xml: it resolves dependencies from Maven Central, runs a fixed lifecycle of phases (compile, test, package, install, deploy) through plugins, and defines the repository format the whole JVM ecosystem shares. Knowing it lets you build and maintain the many Java codebases, including most Spring Boot services, that use it.

glossary.def: Project Object Model: the pom.xml file in a project's top folder. It tells Maven the project's name and version, which libraries it needs, and how to build it.
The three names that identify a Maven project or library: groupId (who makes it), artifactId (what it is) and version, written groupId:artifactId:version.
In Maven, a file stored and shared under its coordinates, usually a JAR plus its pom.xml. Your build produces one; every library you use is one.
In Maven, a store of artifacts (libraries and their POMs) arranged by coordinates: an online one such as Maven Central, or a folder on your own computer.
The folder ~/.m2/repository on your computer where Maven keeps every library it has downloaded or installed, shared by all your projects.
The main public online repository of Java libraries. Maven downloads from it by default, and most open-source Java libraries are published there.
A Maven version ending in -SNAPSHOT, like 1.1.0-SNAPSHOT: work in progress that can be rebuilt and replaced, unlike a release version, which never changes.
A finished Maven version without -SNAPSHOT, such as 1.3.0. Repositories never let it be replaced, so it always means exactly the same files.
A design rule: the tool assumes sensible defaults (such as where source files live), so you only write settings for what is different.
In Maven, a named value in the POM, like a variable, used as ${name}. For example, maven.compiler.release sets the Java version.
A small script (mvnw) kept in a project. It downloads and runs the exact Maven version the project expects, so everyone builds the same way.
In Maven, the setting on a dependency that says when it is needed: compile (the default), test, runtime, provided or import.
A library you get indirectly, because one of your dependencies needs it. Maven adds these automatically.
Maven's fixed, ordered list of build steps (phases), such as compile, test and package. Running one phase runs all the ones before it.
One named step of Maven's build lifecycle, such as compile, test or package. A phase does nothing itself; the plugin goals attached to it do the work.
One command offered by a Maven plugin, written plugin:goal, such as compiler:compile. Goals are attached to phases or run directly.
The Maven plugin that runs unit tests in the test phase. It picks up test classes whose names end in Test.
The Maven plugin that runs integration tests (classes named *IT) and reports their failures in the verify phase.
Bill of materials: a POM that only lists matching versions of many libraries. Importing it lets you leave the versions out of your own dependencies.
A popular Java framework for building web services. It publishes a BOM and a parent POM that many Maven projects use.
A POM whose settings other POMs take over by naming it in a <parent> block, so shared configuration is written once.
In Maven, a POM taking over settings from its parent POM, such as versions and plugin setup, which it can keep or change.
In Maven, one part of a larger build, in its own folder with its own pom.xml. A root POM lists its modules so one command builds them all.
In Maven, a root POM listing its modules in <modules>, so one command builds all of them together.
The part of Maven that collects the modules of a multi-module build, sorts them so each comes after the modules it needs, and builds them in that order.
A Maven build made of several modules (sub-projects) under one root POM, built together with one command.
Your POM as Maven really sees it, with everything from parent POMs and defaults filled in. Print it with mvn help:effective-pom.
A Maven version written as ${revision} in the POM and set from outside, e.g. -Drevision=1.2.0, so a build server can choose it without editing files.
In Maven, a named block of extra POM settings that applies only when switched on: with -P on the command line, or by a condition such as the JDK version.
Your personal Maven settings file (~/.m2/settings.xml), kept outside projects. It holds things like repository passwords and mirrors.
In Maven settings, a rule that sends downloads meant for one repository (often all of them) to another, such as a company's repository manager.
A server a company runs to host its own Maven repositories and keep copies of downloads from Maven Central. Nexus and Artifactory are common ones.
Maven's rule for picking one version when a library is reachable along several paths: the version closest to your POM wins; at equal distance, the first declared.
A setting on a dependency telling Maven not to bring in one of that dependency's own dependencies.
A tool that runs inside the Java compiler and writes extra code based on annotations in your classes. Lombok and MapStruct are examples.
One JAR file containing your classes and all their dependencies, so the app runs with a single java -jar command.
Copying dependencies' classes into your own JAR to make a fat JAR, optionally renaming their packages so they can't clash with other versions.
Java's built-in way for a library to find add-ons while running: each add-on JAR lists its classes in a file under META-INF/services.
In Maven, to upload a built artifact and its POM to a shared online repository (the deploy phase) so other people and projects can download it.
A digital stamp made with your secret key that lets anyone check a file really came from you and was not changed.
A Maven plugin goal written in Java: a class with an execute() method, marked @Mojo to give the goal its name.
A JAR listed in .mvn/extensions.xml that changes how Maven itself works (for example adding a build cache), rather than adding one build step.
The Maven Daemon: a version of Maven that keeps a warmed-up JVM running in the background, so repeated builds start almost instantly.
A build that turns the same source code into exactly the same output bytes every time, so anyone can check that a published file came from that code.
In Maven 4, the simplified POM published with your artifact: final versions filled in and build-only settings removed.
In Maven 4, the pom.xml you write and build with, before Maven turns it into the simpler consumer POM it publishes.

concepts.name: What Maven does and why
concepts.summary: Why real Java projects need a build tool, what libraries and JAR files are, and where Maven gets them from.
concepts.why: Every Maven command makes sense once you know the chores it takes off your hands.
concepts.body:
So far you have compiled programs with `javac` and run them with `java`. That works for a few files. A real project has hundreds of files, uses code other people wrote, and must be built the same way by everyone on the team. Typing those commands by hand stops working fast.

A **library** is ready-made code someone else wrote, such as code that reads spreadsheets or sends email, which you use from your own program instead of writing it yourself. When your project needs a library, that library is one of its **dependencies**. Libraries often need other libraries in turn.

Java libraries are shipped as **JAR** files (Java ARchive): one zip file holding compiled `.class` files. To compile and run code that uses a library, `javac` and the JVM must be told where its JAR is. That list of places to look for classes is the **classpath**, given with the `-cp` option.

**Maven** is a **build tool**: a program that does all of this from one command. You describe your project once, in a file called `pom.xml`: its name, its version and the libraries it needs. Maven then downloads those libraries, compiles your code, runs your tests and packs the result into a JAR of your own.

Where do the libraries come from? A store of published libraries is called a **repository**. The main one is **Maven Central**, a huge public online repository that anyone can download from.

Maven saves every file it downloads in a folder on your computer, the **local repository**: `~/.m2/repository` (`~` means your own user folder). Each version is downloaded only once, and all your projects share it.

Gradle is the other common Java build tool, but Maven is the most widespread, and nearly every Java tool understands its way of naming and storing libraries.
concepts.code:
# By hand: name every library JAR yourself, in every command
# (-cp gives the classpath, -d says where to put the .class files)
javac -cp libs/csv-reader.jar:libs/text-utils.jar -d out src/App.java
java  -cp out:libs/csv-reader.jar:libs/text-utils.jar App

# With Maven: libraries are listed once in pom.xml
mvn package            # download libraries, compile, test, build a JAR
ls ~/.m2/repository    # every library Maven has downloaded so far
mvn --version          # check Maven is installed
takeaways: A library your project needs is a dependency; Java libraries ship as JAR files
Maven downloads dependencies, compiles, tests and builds a JAR with one command
Libraries come from Maven Central and are kept in the local repository, ~/.m2/repository
pitfalls: Copying library JAR files into the project folder by hand; list them in pom.xml and let Maven fetch them.

quiz.q: Your program uses library A, and A itself uses library B. What does Maven do when you build?
options: Downloads only A; you must download B yourself
Downloads A and B and puts both on the classpath
Copies the source code of A and B into your project
Fails, because B is not listed in your pom.xml
quiz.explain: Maven reads what each library needs and fetches those libraries too, so A and B both end up on the classpath.

quiz.q: Where does Maven keep the libraries it has downloaded?
options: Only in memory while it runs
In the local repository, ~/.m2/repository, shared by all projects
quiz.explain: The local repository is one folder per computer, so each library version is downloaded once and reused.

concepts.name: The POM and the mvn command
concepts.summary: Read a small pom.xml, understand the coordinates that name a project, and run the everyday mvn commands.
concepts.why: The POM is the single description of a Maven build; every task starts from it and from the mvn command.
concepts.body:
Maven reads everything about a project from one file in its top folder, `pom.xml`. POM stands for Project Object Model; in practice, "the **POM**" just means this file.

The file is written in **XML**, a text format that wraps each value in named tags: in `<version>1.0.0</version>` the value sits between a start tag and an end tag with a slash. Tags can sit inside other tags to group things, like folders inside folders. Text between `<!--` and `-->` is a comment.

Every project has three **coordinates** that together form its unique name, like a postal address:

- `groupId`: who makes it, usually your organization's web address reversed, like `com.acme`.
- `artifactId`: the project's own name, like `shop-api`.
- `version`: like `1.0.0`. A version ending in `-SNAPSHOT` (`1.1.0-SNAPSHOT`) is a **snapshot**: work in progress that may still change.

Libraries are named the same way, written `groupId:artifactId:version`. Whatever Maven builds or downloads under such a name (usually a JAR plus its POM) is called an **artifact**. The `packaging` tag says what your project produces: `jar` is the default.

Maven follows **convention over configuration**: put files where it expects them and you don't have to tell it anything. Code goes in `src/main/java`, other files your program reads in `src/main/resources`, tests in `src/test/java`, and everything Maven produces in `target/`.

Settings go in `<properties>`. A **property** is a named value in the POM, like a variable. `maven.compiler.release` sets the Java version to compile for, and `project.build.sourceEncoding` tells Maven how your files store letters, so characters like é come out right.

Run Maven in a terminal from the project folder:

- `mvn compile` compiles your code into `target/classes`; `mvn test` also runs the tests.
- `mvn package` does both and builds `target/shop-api-1.0.0.jar`.
- `mvn install` also copies that JAR into your local repository, so your other projects can use it.
- `mvn clean` deletes `target/`; `mvn clean package` is the usual full rebuild.
- Handy flags: `-q` prints less, `-DskipTests` skips tests, `-o` works offline, `-e` shows more detail on errors.

Most projects also include the **Maven Wrapper**: a small **script** (a file of commands you can run) called `mvnw`, plus a `.mvn/wrapper/` folder. Running `./mvnw` instead of `mvn` uses the exact Maven version the project expects, so the whole team builds the same way.
concepts.code:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- The first lines are a standard header: copy them as they are -->
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
  <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

  <groupId>com.acme</groupId>              <!-- the coordinates -->
  <artifactId>shop-api</artifactId>
  <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
  <packaging>jar</packaging>

  <properties>
    <maven.compiler.release>21</maven.compiler.release>
    <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
  </properties>
</project>

<!-- Put your code in src/main/java/App.java, then:
     ./mvnw clean package        -> target/shop-api-1.0.0-SNAPSHOT.jar
     ./mvnw test -q              -> runs the tests in src/test/java
     java -cp target/classes App -> runs your program -->
takeaways: pom.xml describes the project in XML tags
groupId:artifactId:version (the coordinates) names every project and library
Code in src/main/java, tests in src/test/java, output in target/
`mvn clean package` is the everyday full build; use `./mvnw` when the project has it
pitfalls: Building with a different Maven version than your teammates; use the project's ./mvnw.

quiz.q: What does mvn install do beyond mvn package?
options: Copies the built JAR into your local repository (~/.m2) so other projects on your computer can use it
Uploads the JAR to Maven Central
Installs every library on your computer for all programs
quiz.explain: install does everything package does, then puts the JAR and its POM into the local repository.

quiz.q: Where should your main Java code go so Maven compiles it without extra settings?
options: The project's top folder, next to pom.xml
quiz.explain: By convention Maven compiles src/main/java; target/ is output and src/test/java holds tests.

concepts.name: Declaring dependencies and scopes
concepts.summary: List the libraries your project needs in pom.xml, and use scopes to say whether each is needed to compile, to run, or only for tests.
concepts.why: Scopes decide which libraries your code can use while compiling and which ones get shipped with your program.
concepts.body:
To use a library, add a `<dependency>` block with its coordinates inside `<dependencies>` in your POM. On the next build Maven downloads it (unless it is already in your local repository) and puts its JAR on the classpath, so your code can `import` its classes. A library's website usually shows the exact block to paste.

Not every library is needed all the time. A dependency's **scope** says when it is needed:

- `compile` (the default): needed to compile, test and run your code.
- `test`: only for your test code, which checks that the rest works. **JUnit**, the standard Java testing library, belongs here. Test libraries never ship with your program.
- `runtime`: not needed to compile, only when the program runs.
- `provided`: needed to compile, but whatever runs your program already includes it, so Maven leaves it out of what you ship.

A typical `runtime` dependency is a database **driver**: the code that lets Java talk to one particular database. You write your code against Java's general database classes, and the driver is only loaded when the program runs. A typical `provided` one is Lombok, a tool that writes repetitive Java code for you while compiling.

Two more scopes exist: `import`, covered in a later lesson, and `system`, which is outdated; avoid it.

Libraries have dependencies of their own. Maven reads each library's POM and fetches those too. These are **transitive dependencies**: dependencies of your dependencies. You list only what your own code uses directly. A library's `test` and `provided` dependencies are not passed on to you.

Two commands help you check: `mvn dependency:tree` prints everything that was pulled in and through which library, and `mvn dependency:analyze` lists libraries you use without declaring them and ones you declare but never use.

Always write an exact version. Maven also accepts ranges like `[1.2,2.0)`, but then two builds of the same code can pick different versions. Many teams keep version numbers in `<properties>` (`<junit.version>5.11.4</junit.version>`) and refer to them as `${junit.version}`, so each number is written once.
concepts.code:
<properties>
  <junit.version>5.11.4</junit.version>
</properties>
<dependencies>
  <dependency>                               <!-- compile scope (the default) -->
    <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.core</groupId>
    <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>
    <version>2.18.3</version>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>                               <!-- database driver: only when running -->
    <groupId>org.postgresql</groupId>
    <artifactId>postgresql</artifactId>
    <version>42.7.5</version>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>                               <!-- needed to compile, not shipped -->
    <groupId>org.projectlombok</groupId>
    <artifactId>lombok</artifactId>
    <version>1.18.36</version>
    <scope>provided</scope>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>                               <!-- only for tests -->
    <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
    <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
    <version>${junit.version}</version>
    <scope>test</scope>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>
<!-- mvn dependency:tree      mvn dependency:analyze -->
takeaways: Add a library with a <dependency> block holding its coordinates
Scopes: `compile` (default), `test`, `runtime`, `provided`
Dependencies of your dependencies (transitive ones) come automatically; mvn dependency:tree shows them
Write exact versions, ideally once in <properties>
pitfalls: Giving a database driver compile scope, then accidentally writing code that only works with that one driver.

quiz.q: Which scope should the JUnit library have?
quiz.explain: JUnit is only needed to compile and run tests, so test scope keeps it out of the program you ship.

quiz.q: Your code imports classes from library A. A uses library B internally. Which do you list in your POM?
options: Only A; Maven fetches B as a transitive dependency
Both A and B, or the build fails
quiz.explain: List what your own code uses; Maven reads A's POM and brings in B by itself.

concepts.name: The build lifecycle
concepts.summary: See the fixed order of steps (phases) Maven runs, which plugins do the work, and what `mvn package` or `mvn install` really runs.
concepts.why: Knowing the phases explains why `mvn package` also runs your tests, and where extra build steps can go.
concepts.body:
Building a project always takes the same steps in the same order: check the setup, compile, test, pack the JAR. Maven calls this sequence the **build lifecycle**, and each named step in it is a **phase**. The main phases, in order:

1. `validate`: check the POM is complete
2. `compile`: compile `src/main/java`
3. `test-compile`, then `test`: compile and run the tests
4. `package`: pack the JAR
5. `integration-test`, then `verify`: run slower tests of whole parts working together, and check their results
6. `install`: copy the JAR to your local repository
7. `deploy`: upload it to a shared online repository for other people

Running a phase runs every phase before it. So `mvn package` checks, compiles, tests and packs, and `mvn install` does all that and then installs. A separate `clean` lifecycle just deletes `target/`; `mvn clean install` runs it first, then the main lifecycle up to `install`.

Phases are only names. The real work is done by **plugins**: add-on pieces of Maven, each good at one job. A plugin offers one or more **goals** (its commands), written `plugin:goal`. For example, `compiler:compile` compiles your code, `surefire:test` runs tests with the **Surefire** plugin, and `jar:jar` builds the JAR.

Maven attaches ("binds") these standard goals to the right phases for you, based on the project's `packaging`. That's why a bare POM can already compile, test and build a JAR.

You can also run a goal directly, without the lifecycle: `mvn dependency:tree` lists dependencies, and `mvn help:effective-pom` prints your POM with every default Maven fills in.

To add a step of your own, list a plugin under `<build><plugins>` and give it an `<execution>` naming the goal and the phase it should run in. The Configuring plugins lesson shows how.

`-DskipTests` still compiles the tests but doesn't run them; `-Dmaven.test.skip=true` doesn't even compile them.
concepts.code:
# Each phase runs all earlier phases
mvn compile             # validate -> compile
mvn test                # ... -> test-compile -> test      (Surefire)
mvn package             # ... -> package                   (jar plugin)
mvn verify              # ... -> integration-test -> verify
mvn install             # ... -> install  (~/.m2/repository)
mvn clean install       # clean lifecycle first, then up to install

# Goals can be run directly, outside the lifecycle
mvn help:effective-pom          # your POM with every default filled in
mvn dependency:tree             # what libraries were pulled in
mvn surefire:test -Dtest=UserServiceTest   # run one test class
mvn versions:display-dependency-updates    # newer versions of your libraries

# Skipping tests
mvn package -DskipTests          # compile tests but don't run them
mvn package -Dmaven.test.skip=true   # don't even compile them
takeaways: A phase runs every phase before it
Plugins do the work; their goals are bound to phases, with defaults set by the packaging
`verify` adds the slower whole-system tests; `install` copies the JAR to ~/.m2
plugin:goal runs one goal directly

quiz.q: What runs when you execute mvn package?
options: All phases up to package, including compile and test
Only compile and package; tests are skipped
quiz.explain: Phases are cumulative: package runs validate, compile, test-compile, test and then package.

concepts.name: Testing with Surefire and Failsafe
concepts.summary: Run JUnit 5 unit tests with Surefire and integration tests with Failsafe, and choose which tests run.
concepts.why: Running tests is the part of Maven you use most, every day.
concepts.code:
<build>
  <plugins>
    <plugin>
      <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
      <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
      <version>3.5.2</version>
      <configuration>
        <excludedGroups>slow</excludedGroups>    <!-- skip tests marked @Tag("slow") -->
        <systemPropertyVariables>                <!-- tests read it with System.getProperty("app.env") -->
          <app.env>test</app.env>
        </systemPropertyVariables>
      </configuration>
    </plugin>
    <plugin>
      <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
      <artifactId>maven-failsafe-plugin</artifactId>
      <version>3.5.2</version>
      <executions>
        <execution>
          <goals><goal>integration-test</goal><goal>verify</goal></goals>
        </execution>
      </executions>
    </plugin>
  </plugins>
</build>
<!-- mvn test -Dtest=UserServiceTest        -> unit tests only
     mvn verify                             -> unit tests + *IT integration tests
     reports: target/surefire-reports, target/failsafe-reports -->
takeaways: Surefire runs *Test classes in the test phase
Failsafe runs *IT classes in integration-test and reports failures in verify
-Dtest=Class#method picks tests; -DskipTests skips them
Reports land in target/surefire-reports
pitfalls: Naming a slow integration test *Test, so it runs with the fast unit tests on every mvn test.

quiz.q: Why does Failsafe report failures in verify rather than in integration-test?
options: So post-integration-test can still clean up before the build stops
quiz.explain: Waiting until verify lets cleanup goals bound to post-integration-test run first.

quiz.q: A class in src/test/java is called OrderIT. Which command runs it?
options: mvn verify, with Failsafe added to the POM
quiz.explain: *IT classes are integration tests; Failsafe runs them in the integration-test phase, which mvn verify includes.

concepts.name: dependencyManagement and BOMs
concepts.summary: Set library versions in one place with dependencyManagement, import BOMs, and see how managed versions reach transitive dependencies.
concepts.why: This is how Spring Boot and large projects keep hundreds of library versions consistent.
concepts.body:
`<dependencyManagement>` declares versions (and optionally scopes) **without adding** the dependencies. Your `<dependencies>` section then lists only `groupId` and `artifactId` and takes the version from there. Managed versions also apply to transitive dependencies, so managing `jackson-databind` fixes its version wherever it shows up in the tree.

A **BOM** (bill of materials) is a POM that contains only a `dependencyManagement` section: a list of library versions known to work together. Import it with `<type>pom</type>` and scope `import`:

```xml
<dependencyManagement><dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-dependencies</artifactId>
    <version>3.4.4</version>
    <type>pom</type>
    <scope>import</scope>
  </dependency>
</dependencies></dependencyManagement>
```

After that, Spring, Jackson, JUnit and dozens of other libraries can be declared without versions, and they are guaranteed to fit together.

Spring Boot projects more often use `spring-boot-starter-parent` as their **parent POM**: a POM whose settings yours takes over, named in a `<parent>` block (the multi-module lesson explains this). That parent imports the same BOM and also sets up the build. Importing the BOM yourself is the alternative when your project already has a different parent.

Which version wins? A version written directly in `<dependencies>` beats a managed one. Among managed versions, the first declaration in the POM wins, including the order of imported BOMs. `mvn help:effective-pom` shows the final result, and `mvn dependency:tree -Dverbose` shows which versions were managed.
concepts.code:
<dependencyManagement>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>                                       <!-- import a BOM -->
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-dependencies</artifactId>
      <version>3.4.4</version>
      <type>pom</type>
      <scope>import</scope>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>                                       <!-- pin a version everywhere -->
      <groupId>com.google.guava</groupId>
      <artifactId>guava</artifactId>
      <version>33.4.0-jre</version>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<dependencies>
  <dependency>                                         <!-- versions come from management -->
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>com.google.guava</groupId>
    <artifactId>guava</artifactId>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>
takeaways: dependencyManagement sets versions without adding dependencies
Managed versions also override transitive ones
Import a BOM with type pom and scope import
A direct version beats a managed one; the first managed declaration wins

quiz.q: What happens if a dependency is listed in dependencyManagement but not in dependencies?
options: It is added with compile scope
Nothing is added; only its version is fixed if it appears anywhere in the graph
It is added with test scope
quiz.explain: dependencyManagement only manages versions and settings; it never adds a dependency by itself.

concepts.name: Configuring plugins
concepts.summary: Configure plugins in the build section, bind executions to phases, and share settings with pluginManagement.
concepts.why: Compiler flags, packaging, generated code and quality checks are all plugin configuration.
concepts.body:
Plugins are declared under `<build><plugins>` with their coordinates and a `<configuration>` block of settings. Maven's own plugins (group `org.apache.maven.plugins`) can leave out the groupId. Always write the plugin version; otherwise Maven warns and picks a default that may be old.

Key plugins:

- **maven-compiler-plugin**: `<release>21</release>`, extra compiler flags in `<compilerArgs>`, and `<annotationProcessorPaths>` for **annotation processors**, tools such as Lombok or MapStruct that write extra code while compiling.
- **maven-jar-plugin**: entries in the JAR's **manifest**, a small description file inside every JAR, such as `Main-Class` (the class `java -jar` starts).
- **maven-shade-plugin** or **spring-boot-maven-plugin**: build one runnable **fat JAR** that also contains all the dependencies.
- **maven-enforcer-plugin**: stop the build unless rules hold, such as a minimum Maven or JDK version, or no snapshot dependencies.
- **maven-resources-plugin** with `<filtering>true</filtering>`: copies `src/main/resources` and fills in placeholders like `${project.version}`.
- Also common: **exec-maven-plugin** (run a program), **jacoco-maven-plugin** (measure how much code the tests run), **spotless-maven-plugin** (format code).

An `<execution>` binds goals to a phase, with its own `<id>` and configuration; one plugin can have several. Leave out `<phase>` when the goal has a default phase. Run one execution directly with `mvn plugin:goal@executionId`.

`<pluginManagement>` fixes versions and configuration for plugins **without switching them on**; a plugin runs only where it is also listed under `<plugins>`, and then needs no version there. Put it in a **parent POM**, a shared POM that other POMs name in their `<parent>` block and take settings from (next lesson), so every project using that parent gets the same plugin setup.

Configuration values can use properties (`${java.version}`). You can override a setting from the terminal with `-Dname=value` only when the plugin offers a user property for it; each goal's documentation lists them, e.g. `-Dmaven.compiler.release=17`.
concepts.code:
<build>
  <pluginManagement>                         <!-- versions/config for the whole build -->
    <plugins>
      <plugin>
        <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
        <version>3.13.0</version>
        <configuration>
          <release>21</release>
          <compilerArgs><arg>-Xlint:all</arg></compilerArgs>
        </configuration>
      </plugin>
    </plugins>
  </pluginManagement>
  <plugins>
    <plugin>
      <artifactId>maven-enforcer-plugin</artifactId>
      <version>3.5.0</version>
      <executions>
        <execution>
          <id>enforce-versions</id>
          <goals><goal>enforce</goal></goals>     <!-- default phase: validate -->
          <configuration>
            <rules>
              <requireMavenVersion><version>[3.9,)</version></requireMavenVersion>
              <requireJavaVersion><version>[21,)</version></requireJavaVersion>
              <banDuplicatePomDependencyVersions/>
            </rules>
          </configuration>
        </execution>
      </executions>
    </plugin>
  </plugins>
</build>
takeaways: Pin plugin versions under build/plugins or pluginManagement
executions bind goals to phases, each with its own configuration
pluginManagement shares settings without switching plugins on
Compiler, Surefire, jar or shade, and enforcer are the core set
pitfalls: Leaving plugin versions unspecified, so builds change behavior when Maven's defaults change.

quiz.q: What is the difference between plugins and pluginManagement?
options: plugins is for parents, pluginManagement for children
pluginManagement only sets versions and configuration; plugins actually adds the plugin to the build
quiz.explain: Like dependencyManagement, pluginManagement only describes settings; the plugin runs only where it is listed under plugins.

concepts.name: Multi-module projects and parent POMs
concepts.summary: Split a build into modules under a parent POM, share settings through inheritance, and build only the modules you need.
concepts.why: Most real Maven codebases are multi-module builds; inheritance and the reactor are what keep them manageable.
concepts.body:
As a project grows, you split it into **modules**: smaller sub-projects in their own folders, each with its own `pom.xml`, such as `core` and `api`. A root POM with `<packaging>pom</packaging>` lists them in `<modules>` by folder name, and each module usually names the root as its `<parent>`. Two separate mechanisms are at work:

- **Aggregation** (`<modules>`): one command builds every listed module. The **reactor**, the part of Maven that does this, sorts them so each module is built after the modules it needs.
- **Inheritance** (`<parent>`): a module takes over its parent's properties, `dependencyManagement`, `pluginManagement`, repositories and plugins. It only needs its own `artifactId`; groupId and version come from the parent. `<relativePath>` says where the parent's pom.xml is; the default, `../pom.xml` (the folder above), fits the usual layout.

Modules depend on each other with normal `<dependency>` elements, using `${project.version}` as the version. The reactor takes these from the modules built in the same run. In Maven 3 the needed module must be packaged in that run, which is why `mvn install` became the habit; Maven 4 handles this better.

Useful reactor flags:

- `-pl api,core` builds only those modules; `-am` also builds the modules they need; `-amd` also builds the modules that need them.
- `-rf :api` resumes from a module after a failure.
- `-T 4` (or `-T 1C`, one per processor core) builds independent modules **in parallel**, at the same time.

To keep one version across all modules, use **CI-friendly versions**: write `<version>${revision}</version>` everywhere and set it from outside with `-Drevision=1.2.0`. The name comes from **CI** (continuous integration): a server that automatically builds and tests every change, and can now pick the version without editing files. The flatten plugin (or Maven 4) writes the real version into the published POM.

Run `mvn help:effective-pom -pl api` to see the **effective POM**: what a module really ends up with after inheritance and defaults.
concepts.code:
<!-- pom.xml (root / parent) -->
<project>
  <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
  <groupId>com.acme</groupId>
  <artifactId>shop-parent</artifactId>
  <version>${revision}</version>
  <packaging>pom</packaging>
  <properties>
    <revision>1.2.0-SNAPSHOT</revision>
    <maven.compiler.release>21</maven.compiler.release>
  </properties>
  <modules>
    <module>core</module>
    <module>api</module>
  </modules>
</project>
<!-- api/pom.xml -->
<project>
  <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
  <parent>
    <groupId>com.acme</groupId>
    <artifactId>shop-parent</artifactId>
    <version>${revision}</version>
  </parent>
  <artifactId>api</artifactId>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>com.acme</groupId>
      <artifactId>core</artifactId>
      <version>${project.version}</version>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</project>
<!-- mvn -pl api -am package     mvn -T 1C verify     mvn -rf :api install -->
takeaways: modules aggregate (the reactor builds them); parent inherits (configuration)
Modules inherit groupId, version, management sections and plugins
-pl, -am, -amd and -rf choose what to build; -T builds in parallel
Use ${revision} CI-friendly versions to set one version from outside
pitfalls: Changing the parent version and forgetting to update the <parent> block in every module.

quiz.q: What does mvn -pl api -am package do?
options: Builds api and every module it depends on
Builds api and every module that depends on it
quiz.explain: -am (also-make) adds the modules that api depends on to the build.

concepts.name: Profiles, properties and settings.xml
concepts.summary: Vary the build with properties and profiles, and keep personal settings such as passwords and mirrors in settings.xml.
concepts.why: Build servers, private repositories and builds that differ per environment all rely on profiles and settings.
concepts.body:
You've already used properties. Besides your own in `<properties>`, Maven provides many: `${project.version}`, `${project.basedir}` (the project folder), `${env.HOME}` for **environment variables** (named settings the computer hands to every program it starts), and Java system properties. Override any of them from the terminal with `-Dname=value`.

A **profile** is a block of extra POM settings that applies only when switched on. It can add dependencies, plugins and properties. Ways to switch one on:

- Explicitly: `mvn package -Pprod` (or `-P!prod` to switch it off).
- By property: `<activation><property><name>env</name><value>ci</value></property></activation>` matches `-Denv=ci`.
- By JDK version, operating system, or whether a file exists; or `<activeByDefault>true</activeByDefault>`, which is switched off as soon as any other profile is active (a common surprise).

`mvn help:active-profiles` lists what is active. Don't use profiles to build different artifacts under the same version (a `prod` JAR and a `dev` JAR with the same coordinates); keep settings that differ per environment outside the artifact.

**settings.xml** (`~/.m2/settings.xml`, or a global one in Maven's install folder) holds your personal, machine-specific settings and is never stored with the project:

- `<mirrors>`: a **mirror** sends downloads meant for Maven Central (or any repository) somewhere else, usually a **repository manager**: a server your company runs, such as Nexus or Artifactory, that keeps copies of downloads and stores private libraries.
- `<servers>`: **credentials** (a username plus a password or access key) for uploading artifacts or reading private repositories, matched to a repository by `<id>`. `mvn --encrypt-password` stores a password scrambled instead of readable.
- `<profiles>` and `<activeProfiles>` for your own defaults; `<proxies>` for networks where all internet traffic must pass through a gateway server.

Automated build servers usually pass their own settings file with `mvn -s ci-settings.xml` and read passwords from environment variables (`${env.NEXUS_TOKEN}`), so they never appear in files.
concepts.code:
<!-- pom.xml -->
<profiles>
  <profile>
    <id>ci</id>
    <activation>
      <property><name>env</name><value>ci</value></property>   <!-- mvn -Denv=ci -->
    </activation>
    <properties>
      <skipITs>false</skipITs>
    </properties>
  </profile>
  <profile>
    <id>jdk-preview</id>
    <activation><jdk>[25,)</jdk></activation>
    <properties><maven.compiler.enablePreview>true</maven.compiler.enablePreview></properties>
  </profile>
</profiles>
<!-- ~/.m2/settings.xml (not committed) -->
<settings>
  <mirrors>
    <mirror>
      <id>nexus</id>
      <mirrorOf>*</mirrorOf>
      <url>https://nexus.acme.com/repository/maven-public/</url>
    </mirror>
  </mirrors>
  <servers>
    <server><id>nexus</id><username>ci</username><password>${env.NEXUS_TOKEN}</password></server>
  </servers>
</settings>
<!-- mvn verify -Pci        mvn help:active-profiles -->
takeaways: Properties fill in values across the POM; override them with -Dname=value
Profiles add settings conditionally (-P, properties, JDK, OS)
activeByDefault switches off when another profile is active
settings.xml holds mirrors and credentials and stays out of the project
pitfalls: Baking environment-specific values into the artifact through profiles, producing JARs that differ by build machine.

quiz.q: A profile is activeByDefault. You run mvn package -Pci. Is the default profile still active?
options: No: activeByDefault profiles are deactivated when any other profile is explicitly activated
quiz.explain: activeByDefault means 'active unless another profile in the same POM is active', a frequent surprise.

concepts.name: Transitive conflicts and exclusions
concepts.summary: Understand the nearest-wins rule, read dependency:tree output, and fix version conflicts with exclusions and managed versions.
concepts.why: Two versions of one library competing for the classpath cause errors like NoSuchMethodError while the program runs; diagnosing them is a core Maven skill.
concepts.body:
When the same library is reachable along several paths, Maven's **nearest-wins** rule (also called dependency mediation) picks the version whose path from your POM is shortest; at equal depth, the first declaration wins. This can quietly pick an *older* version than another library needs. The program then compiles, but fails while running with `NoSuchMethodError` (a method that version doesn't have) or `ClassNotFoundException`.

Diagnosing:

- `mvn dependency:tree -Dverbose` shows the versions that lost, and why (`omitted for conflict with 2.18.3`).
- `mvn dependency:tree -Dincludes=com.fasterxml.jackson.core` narrows the output.
- `mvn dependency:analyze` finds undeclared and unused dependencies.
- `mvn dependency:list -DoutputFile=...` writes the list to a file for other tools.

Fixing:

- **Manage** the version in `dependencyManagement`: it applies to every path, so it is the cleanest fix.
- **Exclude** a transitive dependency on one path with an **exclusion**: `<exclusions><exclusion><groupId>..</groupId><artifactId>..</artifactId></exclusion></exclusions>`. For example, remove `commons-logging` (an old logging library) and add `jcl-over-slf4j`, a drop-in replacement that passes its messages to SLF4J; or remove an old `log4j`.
- Declare the dependency directly (depth 1) so it is nearest; prefer management over this trick.
- `<optional>true</optional>` on one of your own dependencies stops it from being passed on to projects that use yours.

Watch for **duplicate classes**: the same classes published under two different coordinates, often after a project renamed itself (`javax.*` vs `jakarta.*`, `commons-lang` vs `commons-lang3`). Mediation can't help, because Maven sees two different libraries. The enforcer plugin's `dependencyConvergence` rule and `banDuplicateClasses` (from extra-enforcer-rules) catch these on every build.
concepts.code:
<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.apache.httpcomponents.client5</groupId>
    <artifactId>httpclient5</artifactId>
    <version>5.4.3</version>
    <exclusions>
      <exclusion>                              <!-- drop a transitive on this path -->
        <groupId>commons-logging</groupId>
        <artifactId>commons-logging</artifactId>
      </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.slf4j</groupId>
    <artifactId>jcl-over-slf4j</artifactId>   <!-- bridge replacing it -->
    <version>2.0.17</version>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>

<!-- $ mvn dependency:tree -Dverbose -Dincludes=com.fasterxml.jackson.core
[INFO] com.acme:shop-api:jar:1.0.0-SNAPSHOT
[INFO] +- com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind:jar:2.18.3:compile
[INFO] \- com.example:legacy-lib:jar:1.0:compile
[INFO]    \- (com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind:jar:2.12.7:compile
             - omitted for conflict with 2.18.3)
   Fix for the other direction (an old version winning): pin it in dependencyManagement. -->
takeaways: Nearest path wins, then first declaration; not the highest version
dependency:tree -Dverbose shows the losing versions and why
Fix with dependencyManagement first, exclusions second
Enforcer rules catch convergence and duplicate-class problems on every build
pitfalls: Excluding a transitive dependency that the library actually needs, so the failure only shows up once the program runs.

quiz.q: Your POM depends on A (which needs X 1.0) and B (which needs C, which needs X 2.0). Which X does Maven select?
options: X 1.0, because its path is shorter
quiz.explain: Maven's nearest-wins rule picks the version with the shortest path, X 1.0 via A.

concepts.name: Packaging runnable applications
concepts.summary: Build runnable JARs with the jar, shade or Spring Boot plugins, handle resources and manifests, and avoid the traps of merging JARs.
concepts.why: Shipping a service means producing something that starts with java -jar; each approach has trade-offs.
concepts.body:
A plain `mvn package` JAR contains only your classes: no dependencies, and no `Main-Class` in its manifest, so `java -jar` can't start it. Options for a runnable artifact:

- **Jar plugin + classpath**: set `<manifest><mainClass>` and `<addClasspath>true</addClasspath>`, and copy the dependencies next to it with `dependency:copy-dependencies`. Clean and fast, but you ship a folder.
- **maven-shade-plugin**: merges every dependency's classes into one fat JAR (`java -jar app.jar`); this is called **shading**. Use the `ManifestResourceTransformer` for `Main-Class` and the `ServicesResourceTransformer` to merge `META-INF/services` files. Those files drive Java's **service loader**, the way add-ons such as database drivers announce themselves; unmerged, one JAR's file overwrites the others and the add-ons silently go missing. Shade can also **relocate** (rename) a dependency's packages so they can't clash with another version, which is how libraries bundle dependencies safely. Drop the signature files of signed JARs, as in the example.
- **maven-assembly-plugin** with the `jar-with-dependencies` descriptor: simpler, but merges files naively.
- **spring-boot-maven-plugin** `repackage`: puts the dependency JARs, unchanged, inside a launcher JAR, so nothing needs merging. Its `build-image` goal also builds a **container image**: the app packaged with everything it needs, ready for tools like Docker to run.
- **jlink** and **jpackage** (through plugins) build a cut-down Java runtime with only the parts your app uses, and native installers.

Files in `src/main/resources` are copied into the JAR. Turn on `<filtering>` to fill in `${project.version}` in files like `application.properties`, but keep binary files such as images and fonts out of filtered folders, or filtering will corrupt them.

Set `project.build.outputTimestamp` to get a **reproducible build**: the same source gives a JAR identical down to the last byte, which release and verification tools increasingly expect.
concepts.code:
<build>
  <plugins>
    <plugin>
      <artifactId>maven-shade-plugin</artifactId>
      <version>3.6.0</version>
      <executions>
        <execution>
          <phase>package</phase>
          <goals><goal>shade</goal></goals>
          <configuration>
            <createDependencyReducedPom>false</createDependencyReducedPom>
            <transformers>
              <transformer implementation="org.apache.maven.plugins.shade.resource.ManifestResourceTransformer">
                <mainClass>com.acme.App</mainClass>
              </transformer>
              <transformer implementation="org.apache.maven.plugins.shade.resource.ServicesResourceTransformer"/>
            </transformers>
            <filters>
              <filter>                     <!-- drop signatures of signed dependencies -->
                <artifact>*:*</artifact>
                <excludes><exclude>META-INF/*.SF</exclude><exclude>META-INF/*.DSA</exclude><exclude>META-INF/*.RSA</exclude></excludes>
              </filter>
            </filters>
          </configuration>
        </execution>
      </executions>
    </plugin>
  </plugins>
</build>
<!-- mvn package && java -jar target/shop-api-1.0.0-SNAPSHOT.jar -->
takeaways: A default JAR has no dependencies and no Main-Class
Shade merges classes; use transformers for the manifest and META-INF/services
Spring Boot's repackage nests JARs instead of merging them
Set project.build.outputTimestamp for reproducible JARs
pitfalls: Shading without the ServicesResourceTransformer, so database drivers or other add-ons are not found when the program runs.

quiz.q: Why can a shaded JAR fail to find a database driver that works when run from the IDE?
options: META-INF/services files from several jars overwrote each other instead of being merged
The driver must have provided scope
quiz.explain: Service loader registrations live in files with the same name in every JAR; without the services transformer only one survives the merge.

concepts.name: Deploying and releasing artifacts
concepts.summary: Publish snapshots and releases to shared repositories with distributionManagement, mvn deploy, the versions plugin and release workflows.
concepts.why: Sharing libraries across teams and publishing to Maven Central is a core Maven workflow.
concepts.body:
`mvn deploy` runs the build and then **deploys**: it uploads the artifact, its POM and attached extras (sources, Javadoc) to the repository named in `<distributionManagement>`. The username and password come from the `<server>` in settings.xml whose `<id>` matches.

Snapshots vs releases:

- A `-SNAPSHOT` version can be deployed again and again. Each upload gets a timestamp, and projects that use it check for a newer one (daily by default; `-U` forces a check). Snapshot repositories are for ongoing work.
- A **release version** never changes: repositories refuse to accept it twice. Releases must not depend on snapshots (the enforcer's `requireReleaseDeps` rule checks this).

Releasing means: set the release version, tag it in version control, build and deploy, then move on to the next snapshot version. Tools:

- `versions:set -DnewVersion=1.3.0` and `versions:commit`, scripted in CI. With `${revision}` CI-friendly versions you simply pass `-Drevision=1.3.0`, and the **flatten** plugin writes a concrete version into the deployed POM.
- **maven-release-plugin** (`release:prepare` and `release:perform`) automates the tag-and-bump cycle, with more ceremony.

Publishing to **Maven Central** goes through Sonatype's Central Portal (`central-publishing-maven-plugin`). It requires proof that you own your groupId's name (usually a web domain you control), source and Javadoc JARs (`maven-source-plugin`, `maven-javadoc-plugin`), a complete POM (name, description, url, license, developers, scm) and **GPG signatures** (`maven-gpg-plugin`): a digital stamp proving the files came from you unchanged.

Attach sources with the `jar-no-fork` goal so they are deployed next to the main JAR. Never release from a working copy that has local changes not yet saved in version control.
concepts.code:
<distributionManagement>
  <repository>
    <id>nexus</id>                                  <!-- matches <server id="nexus"> in settings.xml -->
    <url>https://nexus.acme.com/repository/maven-releases/</url>
  </repository>
  <snapshotRepository>
    <id>nexus</id>
    <url>https://nexus.acme.com/repository/maven-snapshots/</url>
  </snapshotRepository>
</distributionManagement>

<build>
  <plugins>
    <plugin>
      <artifactId>maven-source-plugin</artifactId>
      <version>3.3.1</version>
      <executions>
        <execution><id>sources</id><goals><goal>jar-no-fork</goal></goals></execution>
      </executions>
    </plugin>
  </plugins>
</build>

<!-- Snapshot:  mvn deploy                       (1.3.0-SNAPSHOT, repeatable)
     Release:   mvn versions:set -DnewVersion=1.3.0 && mvn versions:commit
                mvn -DskipTests deploy && git tag v1.3.0
                mvn versions:set -DnewVersion=1.4.0-SNAPSHOT
     or with CI-friendly versions: mvn -Drevision=1.3.0 deploy -->
takeaways: mvn deploy uploads to distributionManagement using settings.xml credentials
Snapshots can be replaced and are re-checked; releases never change
Release = set version, tag, deploy, move to the next snapshot
Central requires sources, Javadoc, full POM details and GPG signatures
pitfalls: Releasing a version that still depends on a -SNAPSHOT library, which later disappears or changes.

quiz.q: Why does a repository reject a second mvn deploy of version 1.3.0?
options: Release versions are immutable; only -SNAPSHOT versions may be redeployed
Deploy only works once per day
quiz.explain: Projects rely on a release version always meaning the same bytes, so repositories refuse to overwrite it.

concepts.name: Writing Maven plugins and extensions
concepts.summary: Write a Mojo (a plugin goal in Java) with configurable parameters, bind it to a phase, test it, and know when a core extension fits better.
concepts.why: Custom plugins encode organization-specific build steps; understanding Mojos also demystifies every plugin you configure.
concepts.body:
A Maven plugin is a JAR with packaging `maven-plugin` containing **Mojos** (Maven plain Old Java Objects): one class per goal, annotated `@Mojo(name = "goal", defaultPhase = LifecyclePhase.X)`, extending `AbstractMojo` and implementing `execute()`.

Parameters are fields annotated `@Parameter(property = "greet.name", defaultValue = "World")`. Users set them in `<configuration>` or with `-Dgreet.name=Ada`. To read the build itself, add `@Parameter(defaultValue = "${project}", readonly = true) MavenProject project` (or `${session}` for the whole Maven run, `${mojoExecution}` for this execution).

Maven's own services, such as the one that resolves artifacts, are handed to your Mojo when you mark a field or constructor `@Inject` (older code uses `@Component`). This is **dependency injection**: your class says what it needs, and Maven supplies it.

Mojo flags: `requiresDependencyResolution = ResolutionScope.COMPILE` to receive the resolved classpath, `threadSafe = true` so it may run in parallel builds (`-T`), and `aggregator = true` to run once for the whole reactor instead of once per module.

The `maven-plugin-plugin` generates the plugin descriptor (`META-INF/maven/plugin.xml`) from the annotations at build time. Users apply the plugin like any other, by coordinates; a `<pluginGroup>` in settings.xml lets them use the short `prefix:goal` form.

Testing: `maven-plugin-testing-harness` for unit tests, and **maven-invoker-plugin** to run real sample projects under `src/it` as **integration tests**: complete builds that use your plugin. Log with `getLog()`. Fail with `MojoFailureException` for a problem in the user's build, or `MojoExecutionException` for an unexpected error.

**Core extensions** (listed in `.mvn/extensions.xml`) hook into Maven itself rather than adding a lifecycle step: computing the version from git tags (`maven-git-versioning-extension`), reusing outputs of earlier builds (`maven-build-cache-extension`), or Develocity build scans. Maven 4 keeps the plugin **API** (the classes and methods Maven offers to plugin code) largely compatible, and adds a new one in `org.apache.maven.api`, so plugins written this way keep working.
takeaways: A Mojo is an annotated class with execute(); @Parameter fields are its configuration
defaultPhase binds the goal; ${project} and @Inject give build context
Test with the plugin testing harness and invoker integration tests
Core extensions hook into Maven itself (caching, versioning)
pitfalls: Leaving out threadSafe = true on a plugin that is safe, so Maven prints a warning on every -T build.

quiz.q: How does Maven know which phase a goal runs in when the user doesn't specify <phase>?
options: It runs immediately at configuration time
From the Mojo's defaultPhase in the generated plugin descriptor
quiz.explain: The maven-plugin-plugin writes defaultPhase into plugin.xml, which Maven reads to bind the goal.

concepts.name: Build performance and reproducibility
concepts.summary: Speed Maven up with parallel builds, the Maven Daemon, the build cache and offline mode, and make builds reproducible.
concepts.why: Slow builds waste everyone's time, and builds that differ from run to run can't be trusted; Maven has specific remedies for both.
concepts.body:
Maven builds are often slower than they need to be. Levers, roughly in order of payoff:

- **Parallel reactor**: `-T 1C` builds independent modules at the same time, one thread per processor core. Plugins must be marked thread-safe; Maven warns about the others.
- **mvnd** (the Maven Daemon): keeps a warmed-up JVM running in the background, driven by a small fast-starting command, so startup drops from seconds to milliseconds; it also builds modules in parallel by default. Maven 4 adopts these ideas.
- **maven-build-cache-extension**: a **cache** of each module's outputs, looked up by its inputs (sources, POM, dependencies) and stored locally or on a shared server, so unchanged modules are restored rather than rebuilt. Add it in `.mvn/extensions.xml` and tune `maven-build-cache-config.xml`.
- Skip what you don't need: `-DskipTests` for local packaging, `-o` offline when the local repository already has everything, `-pl`/`-am` for a subset, `-Dmaven.javadoc.skip`.
- Run fewer plugins: enforcer, checkstyle and site generation can move to a separate CI job. Send test output to files (`-Dmaven.test.redirectTestOutputToFile=true`) and tune Surefire's forking for your machine.
- Find what's slow with `-Dorg.slf4j.simpleLogger.showDateTime=true`, or a **profiler** extension (`maven-profiler`) that reports the time spent per plugin and module.

**Reproducible builds**: with `project.build.outputTimestamp` set (`<project.build.outputTimestamp>2026-01-01T00:00:00Z</project.build.outputTimestamp>`, updated at each release), the jar, source and javadoc plugins give every file that fixed date and a fixed order, so the same inputs produce byte-identical artifacts. Write every plugin version, avoid version ranges and `LATEST`, and keep dependency versions stable with a BOM plus the enforcer's `requireUpperBoundDeps` and `dependencyConvergence` rules. `artifact:compare` (maven-artifact-plugin) checks a build against a reference one.

CI tips: cache `~/.m2/repository` between runs, use the wrapper, and pass `--batch-mode` and `--no-transfer-progress` for clean logs.
concepts.code:
# .mvn/maven.config  (defaults applied to every mvn invocation in this repo)
--batch-mode
--no-transfer-progress
-T 1C

# .mvn/extensions.xml
# <extensions>
#   <extension>
#     <groupId>org.apache.maven.extensions</groupId>
#     <artifactId>maven-build-cache-extension</artifactId>
#     <version>1.2.0</version>
#   </extension>
# </extensions>

# pom.xml property for reproducible archives
# <project.build.outputTimestamp>2026-01-01T00:00:00Z</project.build.outputTimestamp>

mvnd verify                                  # Maven Daemon: warm JVM, parallel by default
mvn -o -pl api -am -DskipTests package       # offline, subset of modules
mvn verify -Dmaven.build.cache.enabled=true  # with the cache extension installed
mvn clean verify artifact:compare            # check the build is reproducible
# CI: cache ~/.m2/repository between runs; always use ./mvnw
takeaways: -T 1C and mvnd build in parallel and remove JVM startup cost
The build cache extension restores unchanged modules
project.build.outputTimestamp plus exact versions give byte-identical builds

concepts.name: Maven 4: what changes
concepts.summary: Know what Maven 4 changes: POM model 4.1.0, build vs consumer POMs, subprojects, better multi-module builds and a new plugin API.
concepts.why: Maven 4 is the first major release in a decade; teams maintaining builds need to know what to adopt.
concepts.body:
Maven 4 (released after a long 4.0 beta cycle) still builds Maven 3 POMs but modernizes the core:

- **Model 4.1.0**: a new version of the POM format. Modules can leave out the parent's `version` and `groupId`, and `<subprojects>` replaces `<modules>` (both still work). Projects still built with Maven 3 keep model 4.0.0.
- **Build POM vs consumer POM**: the **build POM** you write (with `${revision}`, parent paths, build plugins) is turned, on install and deploy, into a lean **consumer POM** with final versions and no build details. CI-friendly versions then work without the flatten plugin.
- **Reactor improvements**: modules find each other's output in `target/classes` reliably, so `mvn verify` works across modules without `install`; `-r`/`--resume` resumes a failed build automatically; `-pl` accepts `:artifactId` and the reactor reports missing modules.
- **Parallel builds and the daemon**: `-T` is more robust, and mvnd's ideas are being merged in.
- **Stricter and clearer**: features already marked as outdated now fail or warn earlier (`system` scope, `LATEST`/`RELEASE` versions, missing plugin versions), and error messages are clearer.
- **New plugin API** (`org.apache.maven.api.*`): the classes and methods Maven offers to plugin and extension code, now immutable and with proper objects for the lifecycle and the current run. The Maven 3 API is still supported.
- Maven itself needs Java 17 to run; projects can still compile for older Java versions.

Adoption path: upgrade the wrapper to a 4.x version, run the build, fix warnings about plugin versions and outdated features, then move to model 4.1.0 and `<subprojects>` once everyone on the project uses Maven 4. Check each plugin's compatibility notes; most mainstream plugins already support Maven 4.
concepts.code:
<!-- Maven 4 POM using model 4.1.0 -->
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.1.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.1.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.1.0.xsd">
  <modelVersion>4.1.0</modelVersion>
  <groupId>com.acme</groupId>
  <artifactId>shop-parent</artifactId>
  <version>1.2.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
  <packaging>pom</packaging>

  <subprojects>                      <!-- replaces <modules> -->
    <subproject>core</subproject>
    <subproject>api</subproject>
  </subprojects>
</project>

<!-- api/pom.xml: parent version and groupId can be omitted -->
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.1.0">
  <modelVersion>4.1.0</modelVersion>
  <parent>
    <artifactId>shop-parent</artifactId>
  </parent>
  <artifactId>api</artifactId>
</project>

<!-- ./mvnw wrapper:wrapper -Dmaven=4.0.0   then:  ./mvnw verify  (no install needed across modules) -->
takeaways: Model 4.1.0 adds <subprojects> and an optional parent version/groupId
Build POM vs consumer POM makes ${revision} versions clean
Multi-module builds work without install
New immutable API for plugins; the Maven 3 API is still supported
